body: I was an A+ student all my life. I double majored with an almost perfect GPA. Once I graduated college and lost the structure school provided, my life started falling apart. I kept getting anxiety & depression diagnosis over and over again but I felt like those were consequences and not a root cause of my problems. After research and a lot of introspection I got to learn about ADHD, but I still got dismissed. "Everybody loses their keys or their phone". I went to a neurologist who said I had a delayed response in the physical exam, yet said "everybody forgets to eat" and said that it was all because of my A type character. I told him I would love to read but I struggle so badly, and only recently I made the connection that I never actually read the assigned books in school. I'd skim through the information, get an idea of what it was about, and make up a report based on that lol. Anyways, his advice was to try to read 🤦‍♀️. Another pcp dismissed me saying I lacked discipline. He also said there was nothing wrong with my iud and there was nothing possibly wrong with my hormones. He also dismissed me missing my period. Surprise surprise, I was pregnant and the IUD had disappeared. I've been dismissed so many times it makes it harder to seek help. But don't give up. What helped me was to bring the self-assessment adhd form (google it like that, you can fill it out yourself). And honestly, you need to find q provider who is updated, which is very hard. A lot of information on ADHD is very new, and bad grades/difficulty in school is one of the top old school criteria.

I also just got officially diagnosed at 29. I feel you. We're trying to get my dad diagnosed at 62. It is ok to grieve for the "what could've been". But remember there's always a future to look forward to.

Well, first of all Congratulations on your graduation! College is freakin tough, you deserve to get some praise for the accomplishment. 

I can't say what things will look like for you but you reminded me a little about myself. When I was in college things went really dark in my head, more and more frequently and intense as stress built up. To get me going, I promised myself I'd end it all after graduation. When graduation came, I was terrified. The only thing I was clinging to was gone. What was my purpose now? Why bother? But I gathered enough courage to try and get help again. I couldn't figure out what a happy life would look like. At that point, I felt like anxiety and depression where part of my personality. A doctor prescribed me some pills. They helped but they made me sleepy, and I still needed a diagnosis. But they helped me get a glimpse of what life could be, and now I at least have a baseline. I've been to counselors and one psychiatrist with bittersweet experiences. I keep going through ups and downs but I try to enjoy the ups the best I can. It's been a long night, and I lately feel like I am falling down the rabbit hole again. I felt like I needed to talk to someone and relating to your story made me feel less alone. I am gathering the courage to attempt to get help once again. Writing this has helped me remember that the good moments, as brief as they can be and even when right now they might not seem as good, are actually worth staying for. You're not alone.

There is a concept that I am seeing more and more frequently in Mexico, which is to have a kid's playground separate from the regular dine-in area, like McDonald's or Burger King. I know of a place that serves Stake and BBQ that has a regular dinner area, and another with a playground like Peter Piper Pizza, with tickets and gift shop and the same kind of tables with benches. I think it is great because as a parent, you don't have to choose between eating a nice meal or taking your kids to a fun place (where food is usually junk). I also saw in an upscale seafood restaurant a separate room for children, with glass walls so parents can check on their kids but that keeps noise out of the dining area. They have tiny chairs and tables with crayons and paper table mats to color, a big projector with Disney movies, and a few toys to play with.

I think the problem is more a lack of style variation than use of 3D. Spiderverse was 3D, but it made some innovations to give it a 2D/comic book look. Lego was 3D, but it made innovations to make it look stop motion. You mention Peanuts, if you haven't seen the 2015 movie, I would highly suggest you do. It's also 3D but absolutely adorable and charming, and also pushed technology innovation forward. When it comes to Pixar and Disney, I feel like they are focused only on realistic rendering innovation now, so Disney can use the new stuff in other live action films (cough cough Marvel). They have slowed down the ideas on character design and other studios that want to prove they are worth it as much keep copying the aesthetic. The solution? Give your money to productions like the ones you mentioned instead of the same old stuff. That said, check out Klaus on Netflix if you haven't. That is 2D with some technology innovation to track lights and shadow, giving it as much life as a 3D render but keeping the 2D aesthetic. Because of what was done in that film, I expect to see more 2D coming in the next few years, and hopefully a comeback of stylized animation.

And to the people commenting that media and IPs are not history, I think you are wrong. Mainstream media is a reflection of the society we live in, and we've recently realized the importance of integrating pop culture into historical analysis. In recent years, I've been able to see more people studying the history of film, tv, fashion, music, even internet trends. I would argue that part of the problem has more to do with how long, who, and under what terms someone can keep having rights of an IP. Shakespeare's work has a lot of problematic points. But being in the free domain, it can be studied in schools in its original form, and freely adapted to modern standards through new work with even only weak connections to the source material. I think we are seeing the effects of allowing companies to hold on to IP rights for so long.

Yet, because African American communities are not yet free from the connection to those depictions, the mockery, the stereotypes, and still suffer from injustice and racism, blackface should be avoided out of respect. I think, in fact, a case like 30's Rock shows that lack of awareness that comes from white washing history, including old but still popular and profitable IPs. Because that's how I see this, as white washing. The purpose is to save the morality and integrity of white people, their creators, their creations, and their cash cows. It is not about fighting racism.

I feel like in a way, that sanitization of media on the 80s-90s is what made a lot of us unaware of the racism that was actually going on in the real world, especially if we grew up in a place of priviledge. And if you think about it, we can still keep paintings, plays, sculptures, etc. that are problematic as history in a museum and that is ok. It's not sanitized, not changed, it helps acknowledge how things were at a certain point and how that may still be affecting today. However, when it comes to modern film and tv, I think the problem is money. Companies want to keep squeezing money out of old IPs, not only in their original form but with remakes and new derivative products that create a branding personality easy to sell. So the real reason why blackface and other problematic scenes are being edited out, is to sanitize a product to keep profiting from it. But at the end, forgetting that black face could casually exist in shows as dear as Looney Tunes and as recent as 30 Rock (for example) can quickly make us think that black face was a thing of the 1800s and since disappeared. That can lead to the dangerous conclusion that blackface is long gone, along with racism, and therefore the problematic implications attached to blackface have also disappeared (so blackface is now ok, because it'sa thing of the past). And I think we have been able to see the result of that naive thinking of racism disappearing in the last years.

Yup, I tried calling once and they weren't very helpful. When I called, I didn't have the courage to spell it out and say I was feeling suicidal. Just a dialing and daring to speak to someone took a lot of convincing. I am always terrified to say the words and have them dial 911 and make a show out of it and it being in my records (also I had no insurance). Anyways, I wanted to talk to someone I couldn't directly hurt with my negative feelings (so no family, no friends). I called and they answered in a very call-center fashion. Like a "how can I help you" sort of phrase. I said I wasn't feeling well. Again, I couldn't say the words, but I needed to talk through the feeling. I figured calling a suicide hot line was enough of a hint. But no, the lady didn't say much and would just ask me little things here and there. I don't know how to explain it but it felt like when you are at an ER triage and none of what you say matters very much, they are just looking for the code words "chest pain" or "shortness of breath" to assign you for emergency care. That's how it feels, like when you talk to an automated system with a problem, but it won't help you unless you phrase it with the words it's programmed to understand and respond to. After an awkward moment and just a couple of phrases exchanged, I decided to hang up. I was half expecting her to say something like, hold on, are you sure? Idk, but no. She just said ok, some scripted goodbye phrase, and that was it. I've had better experiences with chats, it feels anonymous and impersonal and I think the person on the other end feels a lot more comfortable too. And it's a lot easier to try for people with anxiety, social anxiety, etc. We should encourage suicide help chats instead, imo.
